aether · research log

The instrument before the picture

We set out to build a character pipeline an agent could author — describe a creature, get something riggable, animated, and drawn. The pictures came. What made them come was building the measuring instruments first, and then believing them over our own conclusions.

voxel reconstruction skinning non-photorealistic rendering GPU pass budgets

Chapter one

A volume is a better interface than a mesh

The engine this runs on, aether, is built as a thin native substrate that owns I/O, the GPU and audio, and hosts a WebAssembly runtime. Everything above it is an actor — a component that talks to its peers only by mail. The renderer in this document is one of those components: it can be swapped into a running engine without a relink, and it is driven entirely by messages.

That shape mattered for the research, because it let an agent drive a live engine directly: spawn it, load a component into it, mail it a subject, read the frame back. Every picture below came out of that loop.

The pipeline's target shape was images → scalar occupancy volume → low-poly mesh. The volume in the middle is the load-bearing choice. It is the interface: a person can sketch a world as pictures, an agent can reach the same container through prose without learning a bespoke grammar, and a reconstruction from real photographs fills it too. A finished mesh cannot do that — it arrives at the end of the authoring pathway instead of feeding it.

Holding that line cost us a tempting shortcut later, and it was worth it.

Chapter two

Measure the thing before you build the thing

A predecessor project already ran end to end. It turned a turntable of generated views into per-view depth, solved a joint gauge across them, carved a voxel volume and marched a surface. It produced a recognisable character with real concavity. Then it stalled, and the failure was reported as an algorithm problem. Two different fusion strategies were built to fix it. Both lost to the naive carve.

So the next project built no reconstructor at all until it could answer one question: what do the inputs have to be?

First, ground truth, split by job. A generalised winding number for classification — occupancy, topology, flood fill. A signed distance field for surface placement. One field cannot do both: the winding field saturates and carries no sub-voxel position at all.

Then three ceilings, all measured before any reconstruction was attempted: a geometric one in world units, a visibility one (how much surface is ever seen), and a topological one — which turned out to sit at the noise scale and was demoted to a diagnostic rather than a score.

And then the actual deliverable of the phase: an input budget. Tolerances on per-view gauge error, per-pixel depth noise, and mask boundary accuracy, each expressed as a fraction of the subject's own extent. Three properties of that budget shaped everything after it. Gauge error costs about twice what noise does at equal magnitude. Mask error is asymmetric — eroding a silhouette is catastrophic, dilating it is nearly free, so the rule is err outward when uncertain. And the whole envelope is roughly two orders of magnitude tighter than anything available off the shelf delivers.

With the budget in hand, the predecessor stopped being a mystery. Its inputs, after its own gauge solve, were more than an order of magnitude outside the envelope. That explains the failure completely. It was never the algorithm, and no third fusion strategy would have saved it.

Two fusion strategies were built to fix a data problem. A budget would have been cheaper than either.

Views are chosen to carve, not to see

The most useful correction of the phase. We had a visibility ceiling that measured how much of the surface any camera rig could see, and we read it as a proxy for how much free space the rig could observe. Those are different quantities, and we conflated them for eight consecutive experiments. One rig reported 99.9% surface coverage while leaving well over a third of a cavity unexcavated.

Once measured properly, the elevation of the camera ring turned out to have a genuine optimum with failure on both sides. Too shallow and a cup's cavity fills in solid, because nothing ever looks inside it. Too steep and the cameras start seeing through openings — a teapot's lid annulus — and carve away the body behind them.

Two disciplines that kept paying

We measured a noise floor from grid alignment alone, and made every claim quote its margin against it. Two earlier "findings" died on contact with that rule, which is exactly what it was for.

And: anything denominated in voxels is a resolution confound unless the quantity is genuinely grid-relative. That one bit us three separate times — an error measured in voxel units, a truncation band, and a thickness reach — before it became a habit to catch.

Knowing when to stop

Reconstruction settled on graded accumulation: each view contributes a truncated signed distance, the contributions are weighted and averaged, and the result is thresholded once. It beats a unanimous carve on every subject and, crucially, never shatters — the carve fragments worse as views are added, which is precisely the failure the predecessor reported.

Then the finding that capped the whole effort: decimation is a low-pass filter. Below about a thousand triangles, a reconstruction sits within a few to seventeen per cent of a perfect volume and is visually indistinguishable from it. At game-asset budgets, accuracy work has sharp diminishing returns. That is a licence to stop, and it is worth having in writing.

What broke
Eight experiments read a visibility ceiling as an occlusion ceiling. Two "findings" published without a noise margin. Voxel-denominated quantities confounded with resolution, three times.
What held
Winding number for classification, distance field for placement. Graded accumulation over any voting carve. An input budget that retired the predecessor's failure as a mystery.

Chapter three

Asking generative models for geometry

With a budget, the interesting question became answerable: can any generative source supply images inside it? We ran it as a bake-off with three arms and a scorer that could accept or reject a sample automatically.

Re-prompting a single image for new viewpoints failed, and failed replicably across two different frontier image models. The gauge error came back two orders of magnitude over budget while identity controls came back sub-pixel. The diagnosis is clean and, in hindsight, obvious: these models hold geometry; they do not hold a camera. They will happily draw the same creature again, and they will not put the lens where you asked.

Generated turntable video split the verdict, and the split was the useful result. Conditioning on reference views of the subject fixed identity outright — drift fell to the doorstep of the mask budget, from more than an order of magnitude outside it in the predecessor era. But not one generation delivered the full rotation it was asked for. They rock, they teleport, they pendulum back. The best single take covered a little over a third of a turn.

So camera coverage stopped being a prompting problem and became a purchasing one. The working recipe pairs reference-conditioned generation with rejection sampling, because the pose-fit scorer is an automatic acceptance test — and with an interpolation chain that pins first and last frames, which makes coverage true by construction. A chain failure localises to a single regenerable segment costing about a dollar.

The third arm was a single-image 3D prior, and we dropped it deliberately. It works. It also hands back a finished mesh, which replaces the authoring pathway instead of feeding it. The volume is the product; a shortcut that removes the interface is not a shortcut.

What the arm taught that outlived it

  • Error lives where the model extrapolates and vanishes where it is anchored. Every quality number we have is really a statement about anchoring.
  • N samples of one model are one painter. Averaging kills variance and never touches a shared bias. Only an outside anchor bounds that.
  • Prompting moves yield. It never moved gauge, not once.
  • Drop unreliable witnesses; do not re-interpret them. We had a tidy hypothesis that a mislabelled view could be relabelled and recovered. It was refuted outright. Discarding the view was strictly better.
  • Anything time-shaped backfires. Timed waypoints made results worse. So did negation in prose — asking for the absence of a thing reliably summons it.
What broke
Single-image view synthesis, two models, two orders of magnitude over. Every request for a full rotation. A hypothesis that an unreliable view could be rehabilitated.
What held
Reference conditioning for identity. Frame pinning for coverage. Rejection sampling against an automatic scorer. Refusing the shortcut that would have deleted the interface.

Chapter four

The wall: bad depth is worse than no depth

Here is the number that organises the rest of the project. A carve that uses only silhouettes is method-limited: past a certain point, better input stops helping, because a silhouette simply cannot describe a concavity. A graded accumulation with true depth lands more than an order of magnitude closer to the ceiling. That gap is the entire pipeline. So the depth channel is the binding constraint, and has been ever since.

We tested every accessible depth source — the strongest monocular estimators, a metric-depth model, a diffusion-based one, and frontier image models simply asked for a depth map. All of them, on perfect renders, under oracle per-frame alignment, which is the most generous reading physically available, landed one to two orders of magnitude outside the budget. The image models were the most instructive failure: they return pixel-locked iconography, a bright subject with an edge vignette. It looks like a depth map. The values carry no measurement whatsoever.

The residual is the interesting part. It is relief compression at the scale of body parts. Correlation with truth is above 0.98 and the surface is still several per cent of extent wrong. It follows anatomy. No family of global gauge corrections recovers it. And it is one model's shared bias, so the fusion machinery we had already built — which kills variance beautifully — cannot average it away.

Then the result that hurt: feeding estimated depth into the carve made it dramatically worse than using no depth at all. Not marginally — the estimator-fed carve landed well below the silhouette-only floor. Bad depth does not sharpen a carve; it shatters it. Gating on the model's own confidence improved things and never crossed the floor, which is unsurprising once measured: the confidence barely tracks the error at all.

We verified the meter in both directions before believing that negative. Injected noise of known magnitude read back at its true magnitude; a pure affine change read back as zero. The instrument was sound. The verdict stands.

The one thing that worked: two witnesses

The reframe that got the depth channel moving at all was to stop treating the estimator as a source of measurements and treat it as a witness under cross-examination.

The credible witness — silhouettes — does not measure the cavity, but it does partition the scene: territory it vouches for as solid, territory constrained at the rim, and territory it cannot speak to. The estimator is then permitted to speak only in unvouched territory, only in one direction (it may excavate, never add), and only past a threshold calibrated from its own geometrically impossible negative tail — error it must be making, since it claims material outside the hull.

On the hardest subject that walked the error down by a third, and the guarded version left a single false voxel in a single component. It is not enough to ship the cavity lane. It is the first arrangement in which an out-of-budget estimator was useful rather than harmful.

What broke
Every off-the-shelf depth source, by one to two orders of magnitude, under the most generous possible reading. Confidence gating as a rescue. The hope that fusion could average out a shared bias.
What held
Partition the scene with the credible witness; let the unreliable one speak only where it is unopposed, one-sided, past a threshold measured from its own impossible claims.

Chapter five

The failure that ate a conclusion

This is the chapter we would most want another team to read, because nothing about it was a coding error and every number in it was correct.

Our camera rig sampled several elevation rings at the same set of azimuths. Neat, symmetric, easy to reason about. It also means that the views sharing an azimuth are looking down nearly the same line — so on a vertical wall, forty cameras collapse onto eight distinct tangent directions. Five views agreeing was one witness wearing five hats.

Every corroboration statistic we had was inflated by it. When the rings were re-phased so no two shared an azimuth, honest carvability fell by more than half. The false-carve count halved too, in the good direction, which is how we knew the new rig was better and the old numbers had been flattering.

The expensive part was what the inflated statistics had convinced us of. We had found a repeatable feature in the evidence — a raised boss along the subject's axis — and built a completion rule around it, with a gate to detect it and a profile to exploit it. Re-phased, the feature almost entirely vanished. It had been substantially an artifact of the rig, geometrically simple in rig coordinates and meaningless in the subject's. Our gate, correctly, now stays silent.

The measurements all stood. The stories did not. And the fix cost nothing: phase-staggered rings buy all forty directions for exactly zero additional images.

A symmetric rig is a correlated rig. If your witnesses are arranged neatly, check whether you have as many as you think.

And a related trap, in the other direction

Late in the arc we ran the finished detector on frames from generated video. It carved away over half of a subject that has no cavity at all — a catastrophic false positive on a control.

The cause was that pose error from generated frames is not noise, it is a systematic warp. Every defence we had was built against noise: coherence checks and cross-view corroboration waved the warp straight through, because a consistent lie is coherent. The fix was a pre-gate that measures cross-view residual against the budget directly and refuses the input outright. Clean renders pass it at zero cost; the generated chain misses by a factor of seventy and is turned away at the door.

Chapter six

She moves

With generated views still out of budget for depth, the character lane took a different supply route: treat a commercial image-to-3D service as raw material rather than as a product, and keep the volume as the thing being authored.

That needed one trick to work at all. Stylised anime input reads as flat, and the reconstruction comes back a featureless mask. Ask instead for an unpainted clay figurine with sculpted relief, in the image itself, and eyes, lids, nose and mouth survive all the way through voxelisation. Put the relief in the subject, not in post.

Then the rig: harmonic weights solved over the volume, a small bone set — neck, three-axis head, jaw, two ears — and a control vector to drive them. Two lessons arrived immediately and neither is obvious. Rig completeness dominates: a limb that is not a bone has its flesh bind to whatever is nearby, so legs that lack bones end up welded to the head. And any disconnected fragment — a stray wisp of hair — has no bone within reach, gets all-zero weights, and turns the solve into NaN.

Six rungs of being wrong about deformation

To deform a volume you need, for each cell in the posed shape, the material that arrives there — which means inverting the skinning map. For harmonic linear-blend skinning on a limb shell, the obvious pointwise fixed-point iteration provably diverges. That kicked off six rungs of alternatives.

A chart-based inversion kept the skin's shape and quietly deleted material. A cellular automaton in which defects identify themselves and pull matter through the flesh conserved mass exactly and deviated from the intended shape by precisely the amount the skinning model lies about volume. Neither dominated; the tradeoff was real and worth naming. The winner was a hybrid — the chart result as a tension membrane, its holes as attractors, mass moved by the local rule. Crack counts across the arc went from over two thousand, to seven hundred, to a hundred and seventeen, to thirty-five, with mass conserved.

And then a change of direction made most of that machinery optional. If the deliverable is an agent authoring animations — "make a walk cycle" should simply work — then the core has to be a memoryless pose→skin function: randomly accessible, no frame depending on the last, so a bake is curves rather than frames. The stateful automaton demotes to bounded garnish for jiggle and drag. In hindsight, every hard problem in those six rungs came from taking one enormous jump; integrated small steps are always well-conditioned.

A trot then turns out to be about ten lines of rig curves, with the gait authored in foot space — stride, lift, cadence — and closed-form two-bone inverse kinematics converting that back to hip and knee curves.

Two defects worth stealing

Hard-thresholding a skinning weight to zero puts a C1 kink along every bone's support boundary. When that bone moves, the kink becomes a crease in the displacement, and the surface extractor aliases it into visible stair-steps. The detector we had — a check on the gradient magnitude of the distance field — is structurally blind to it: it polices slope, and a crease is a discontinuity in curvature. Shading exposed what the geometry test could not. Gradient tests catch cliffs, not creases.

A seam between two charts is physical, not numerical. Two charts reconstruct the same surface displaced by roughly the weight gap times the displacement. We spent real time trying to resolve it away. Resolution fixes below-lattice detail; it never fixes two computations disagreeing with each other. The fix was to stop having two charts wherever the pose allows one.

What broke
Pointwise inversion of the skinning map, provably. A weight prune that looked free and shipped a shading crease. Resolution as a cure for a seam. Six rungs' worth of machinery, made largely optional by a change of framing.
What held
Rig completeness before rig quality. A memoryless pose→skin core with the bake as curves. Gait authored in foot space. Small integrated steps over one big jump.

Chapter seven

The face, where taste beat derivation

Faces broke every rule we had established, because a face is where a viewer's tolerance collapses. The eye region alone took several complete redesigns, and the useful record is what the failures had in common.

A blink is not an interpolation. Lerping between an open field and a closed one produces a dissolve — the lid fades out where it is and fades in where it lands, which reads as a ghost, not a movement. A blink has to be motion, a coordinate warp that slides the sculpt's own lid down its own surface, and then a settle, crossfading to a separately generated eyes-closed sculpt so the resting crease is real geometry rather than a squashed approximation of it. A warp squashes what a real closure folds.

Fabricating an eyeball fights the socket and loses. Every attempt to fit an analytic sphere into the eye region failed on inspection — bulging, deleting the lid overhang, capping against the wrong rim. The seat position had to come from a generated sculpt of the same character with the eyes blanked, registered onto the original. Related and painful: seat failures are invisible from the front and obvious at three-quarter and steeper. Never clear a change like that from the view that flatters it.

And the one that generalises furthest. The boundary of the eye aperture needed to be derived from the geometry. We tried seven derivations. Every one failed on the eye, for a different reason each time. It was finally settled by drawing the boundary by hand on an orthographic canvas and lifting it through a deterministic transform. Some boundaries are authored, not derived, and recognising which kind you are holding saves days.

The move that dissolved the whole problem

The face carried its detail all along — lash shelf, iris disc, the parting line of the lips — as relief finer than one cell of the working lattice. Resampling into the volume low-passed it away, and every fix we attempted was an attempt to reconstruct information we had thrown out one step earlier.

The answer was the high-poly bake split that real-time graphics has used for twenty years, pointed at our own pipeline: keep the source surface as the high-poly and the volume as the carrier, and re-inject the fine detail at shading time. Per pixel, find the exact closest point on the source surface, take the difference between its fine normal and the carrier's smoothed one, and add it back. No registration is needed, because the source mesh is the lattice's own ancestor and they already share a world frame.

An unwelcome result about our own metric

A surface-error metric had been our arbiter for months. On one completion problem it ranked a particular result best. Looking at the render, that result was plainly the worst of the set — and the human judgement was correct. The metric priced under-carving against over-carving at a ratio nothing about perception supports.

A related observation from the same session, on generated imagery generally: models trained toward benchmarks that reward complexity over coherence fractalise detail. It is the same disease our metric had. Where the two disagree, the eye holds the definition of real, and the metric is the thing under test.

Chapter eight

Drawing, rather than shading

The renderer asks a different question from a shading pipeline. Not what colour is this pixel, but which lines would an illustrator draw. It began as a pen-plotter renderer emitting vector paths, and that constraint is why it generalised.

The central finding is a simplification. One operation produces every feature. Silhouette, hatch and crease are all level sets of a per-vertex scalar: the view-dot-normal at zero, the position along an axis at multiples of the hatch spacing, and surface relief at a threshold. There is no second extractor anywhere in the renderer.

  • Interpolated crossings beat edge walks. Taking the silhouette as a zero crossing through triangle interiors gives a smooth line. Collecting front/back-facing edge pairs follows the facet boundary and gives a saw.
  • Welding is what makes it a drawing. Level sets arrive as one segment per triangle crossed. Styled unwelded, a pressure taper turns every stub into a lens and the image is dust. Endpoints weld by exact equality because the crossing always interpolates from the lower vertex index — order the interpolation and the seam closes in the last bit.
  • Hatch planes must be global, not per-part. Cut every region by one world-space family and neighbouring arcs are co-planar and weld into a single long stroke. Per-part families land at each part's own latitudes and read as corduroy. World space also keeps the strokes welded to the figure under an orbit instead of sliding across it.
  • Depth cannot separate a hair seam from an eyelid; a material field can. Both are carved equally deeply, so a relief threshold inks all of the hair too. Masking creases by material label did in one filter what two tuned thresholds could not — and the steepness filter we added chasing the same goal was cutting the very lid lines it was meant to keep.

Then colour, as water

Watercolour over the ink was built as a placement rulebook rather than a look, one rule at a time, because hand-placed washes had no answer to the question "why there".

R1
The region is the target; the line is a cutting guide. The mask comes from the material map, never from the wash's own outline.
R2
Value decides coverage — reserve the lit areas. The same tone function drives the hatching, so the two media agree instead of arguing.
R3
Care follows attention: tight and deliberate at the face, loose where the hair falls.
R4
Gesture follows form. Flow direction is taken from the ink's own structure tensor.
R5
Accents are authored policy with derived placement — warmth only where blood is.
R6
Atmosphere extends a region's gesture past the silhouette.

Four findings underneath those rules did the real work. Ink frees paint from boundary duty — which is why looseness is affordable at all. Wash carries low-frequency form and hatch carries the high, a frequency split that stops the two media fighting. Edge fate is a semantic channel: a hard rim says these are different things, a lost edge says these are one thing. And a painted feature is a material — the iris is a meta-material running through the same wash machinery as any baked label, not an ad-hoc coloured stamp. Removing a paint policy has to remap its region to the parent material; deleting it left a mouth-shaped hole in the skin.

Chapter nine

Sixty frames a second, and six lying instruments

Offline the renderer took its time. In the engine it had to hold a frame budget, with headroom, while the character animated. The port graduated into a component (aether-puppet): ink as ribbon geometry, the wash as its under-painting, driven by aether.puppet.load, .look and .pose mail.

One constraint shaped the whole design. Overlay passes draw after the main pass, so the washes cannot be overlays — they have to ride the depth-tested material pass a hair behind the ink plane, letting the depth test keep the ink on top.

The starting point was a static frame comfortably inside budget, an orbiting frame roughly three times over it, and a wash that took half a second to develop, hidden behind a settle gate so it only ran when the camera stopped. It finished at 14.7 ms static — over 60 fps with the wash developing every single frame, producing a byte-identical picture to the gated version, and with orbit down from 66 ms to 41.6 ms. The settle gate is gone.

Almost all of that came from one measurement. Per-pass GPU timestamps showed a single blur shader accounted for 372 of 519 passes and 90.8% of GPU time, while the pass boundaries we had been optimising against were a small fraction of the frame. With the real distribution in hand the fixes were straightforward: sweep only the extent each chain actually needs, change the blur's border handling from clamp to a half-sample reflection (clamp is not preserved by filtering, so an iterated chain and a fused one disagree at the edges), and fuse three box iterations into one piecewise-quadratic kernel per axis — with reflection, the fused kernel is the iterated chain.

Six of our instruments lied to us during this one arc. Every wrong turn in it was an act of faith in a number.

Each lie was caught by disagreeing with a different instrument, never by reasoning harder about the first one.
#What we believedWhat was actually true
1 WebAssembly was carrying a huge performance tax. The packaging task defaulted to a debug wasm build. It exaggerated by about 7×.
2 A GPU dispatch cost ~53 ms. Capturing a frame right after a dispatch blocks on the device queue. Against a cold control the same work measured 6 ms.
3 Something in the executor still cost ~53 ms. The test harness's synchronous PNG encode, billing by image entropy — 37.9 ms for a dense image against 1.9 ms for a flat fill, with identical geometry.
4 CPU bind-group setup cost ~17 ms. Over-attributed by roughly 20×. Making the executor allocation-free was correct and moved almost nothing; the cost was GPU-side render-pass boundaries.
5 One pass cost 11–13 ms. A one-sample priming row. Per-pass moving averages only update on frames where the pass actually ran. Real cost: 3.2 ms.
6 Every whole-frame number collected to that point. The pacing harness never sent a window-size message, so the easel never initialised. None of those frames had any paint in them at all.

And one more that reframes GPU profiling in general: naive begin-to-end pass spans are wrong by more than an order of magnitude, because the GPU keeps many passes in flight. Individual rows are charged marginal time and only the total is meaningful. Two rules came out of the arc and both are cheap to adopt: never time through your observation apparatus, and always read the sample count next to a moving average.

The discipline that made the whole port safe was parity: every stage was gated against the original CPU implementation for a byte-identical frame. That caught a genuine porting bug no performance test would have — a running-sum blur drifting epsilon-negative, then raised to a fractional power, yielding NaN and silently leaving one material unpainted.

Chapter ten

Where it stands

The depth channel is still the binding constraint. Silhouettes alone cannot describe a concavity, and every estimator we can reach is out of budget by one to two orders of magnitude. The most promising direction is a genuinely uncorrelated second witness whose errors are unlike a monocular network's, deployed inside the partition scheme from chapter four rather than as a standalone source. That work is in progress and the outcome is not known.

Meanwhile the lanes that do work are honest about their scope. Convex and solid subjects reconstruct well enough to ship. Cavity subjects are better than they were and not yet good enough. Generated input is correctly refused by the pre-gate rather than silently accepted, which is the behaviour we want from a pipeline that cannot yet trust its own inputs.

On the rendering side the next step is to make the wash breathe with gravity — water travelling down the page laying pigment as it goes, held in frame-persistent GPU state. Full fluid simulation is deliberately out of scope; the goal is the behaviour a painter exploits, not the physics underneath it.

And the direction that ties back to the beginning: an affect channel. When an agent puppeteers a character it could emit a feeling the way it emits reasoning, and the rig maps that feeling onto the control vector — ears, lids, gaze, jaw, head — without hand-authoring channels each time. That is the version of this pipeline worth building, and the reason the volume stayed the interface.

In closing

What we would tell another team

  1. Build the measuring instrument before the thing being measured. A budget converts "it doesn't work" into a number, and a number retires mysteries. Ours retired an entire predecessor project in an afternoon.
  2. Instruments need positive and negative controls before their numbers are believed. Six of ours lied inside one arc. Three separate "findings" died to uncontrolled instruments. Calibrate in both directions — inject a known error and confirm it reads back.
  3. Measure the system, not the instrument. Never time through your observation apparatus, and read the sample count next to every average.
  4. Check whether your witnesses are independent. A symmetric sampling arrangement is a correlated one. Averaging kills variance and never touches a shared bias.
  5. Drop unreliable witnesses; do not re-interpret them. Partition the problem so the unreliable source speaks only where nothing better can, in one direction, past a threshold measured from its own impossible claims.
  6. Some boundaries are authored, not derived — and where a metric and a trained eye disagree about a picture, the metric is the thing under test.

aether

aether is a substrate-and-actors application harness for rapid game development, written in Rust. The renderer described here runs on it as a WebAssembly component. Source and design records, including the architecture decision records referenced throughout, are at github.com/iamacoffeepot/aether.

The reconstruction research is developed in a separate repository. Figures in this document are rendered output from that work; specific tolerances, model rankings and unpublished results are held back.
